In those quaint days, of course, virtually every publisher strove to become a shark rather than a minnow. These days, however, affinity and intentionality are often more important brand attributes than pure scale—particularly in the Google Zero era. As Wired global editorial director Katie Drummond told Axios, “Ultimately, I am very comfortable with the idea that Wired’s audience in the future is a smaller audience, but we want that audience to be loyal.” Like Front Office Sports C.E.O. Adam White, Drummond isn’t expecting the app to fuel an explosion in new subscriptions. Rather, she’s looking at how an app can serve as a clubhouse for the brand’s most engaged audience—a platform for push notifications to boost engagement, and perhaps even serve as a launchpad for new business lines as traditional social and search traffic continue to collapse. Around the same time Mark Zuckerberg was creating Facebook, @ben — writer, founder, investor, and tech builder — was creating an open source social network.

Instead of becoming a billionaire, Ben set about building technology with the potential to make the world more informed and equal.

He describes in our latest newsletter what that decades-long journey has looked like, and where everything’s heading: AI, local journalism, the open social web, and more.

https://newpublic.substack.com/p/why-this-platform-is-for-everyone

So here you get a choice between are they engaging, like are they the kind of posts that people interact with, or are they constructive? Are they kind of what's called bridging posts that actually show you something that you wouldn't normally see? And you can even mess around with how much politics you want in your feed. Imagine that, getting max politics or no politics. So, this is really cool. And the coolest thing is that you can go to \"Why am I seeing this?\" and it'll show you the stuff at the top of your feed and the scores that it got which ranked it at the top. I've never seen anything like this before and it's a really cool project called MySky and it's from researchers Jonathan Stray, Renée DiResta, and Glen Weyl.
